catalog_quote: Stress is lexically determined in Arguni and can fall on any syllable (see the examples in 15). Penultimate stress is the most common. (16) shows two stress minimal pairs. (15) Final stress: mardené [mar.de."ne:] ‘in three days’ / Penultimate stress: uririá”ir [u.Ri."Rja.P:ir:] ‘ancestors’ / Antipenultimate stress: putíggyafwa [pu."ti.é:a.Fwa:] ‘beach’ / Preantipenultimate stress: aérafai [a."e:.Ra.Fa.ji] ‘cannot’ (16) ússu ["Pu.s:u:] ‘penis’ / ussú [Pu."s:u:] (trucated form of ussúfir ‘you go down’ or of ussú’e ‘you (don’t) like’) / gána ["ga:.na:] ‘I am’/‘I am from’ / ganá [ga."na:] ‘I put’ ... Some verb lexemes specify that stress must fall on the first-attaching prefix, e.g. -ssa ‘go up’. This may be a prefixing CV reduplicant (§4), e.g. sé~ssa ‘plact-go up’, a subject prefix (§11.1.1), e.g. gá-ssa ‘1sg-go up’ or the pluractional prefix fa- (§11.2.1), e.g. fássa ‘partpl-go up’. [fn. 15] Such verbs must always have some prefix.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is a lexical property of each word (contrastive: minimal pairs ússu/ussú, gána/ganá) and may fall on the final, penultimate, antepenultimate or pre-antepenultimate syllable; the penult is the most frequent position. A class of verbs (e.g. -ssa 'go up', -agin 'give', ná 'put') lexically requires stress on the first prefix attached to the root (subject prefix, pluractional fa-, or a CV reduplicant). Stress is marked orthographically with an acute accent in the thesis.
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs whose lexical specification places stress on the first-attaching prefix rather than the root (fn. 15: such verbs must always carry a prefix); plural-possessor suffix -si moves the stress (p. ~35, §on possessive affixes); the only attested case of stress on a suffix noted in one lexeme; partial reduplication targets the stressed syllable and keeps penultimate stress in prefix-stressed verbs (§4.1); unstressed final syllables are subject to deletion/syncope (§3.4.4). Words without an acute in the wordlist are either prefix-stressed verbs or not yet transcribed for stress (Appendix A note).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the author states that Arguni lexemes consist of segments plus 'information about the position of the word stress' (§3, p. 11); examples are citation-form words and inflected verbs; possessive particles are described as usually unstressed in the phrase.
new_statements.identity_note: Milano 2025 describes the Arguni (Táfer) variety spoken in Arguni village on Arguni Island, i.e. argu1237 itself, which he treats as one member of the Arguni-Mbaruan-Yarikman (= Glottolog 'Nuta', bomb1263) dialect/language group alongside Mbaruan (Bedoanas, bedo1237 / ISO bed) and Yarikman (Erokwanas, ISO erw). Data from fieldwork Dec 2024 - Feb 2025 in Arguni village. Note Glottolog 5.3 classifies Arguni under Tanimbar-Bomberai > Nuta, not SHWNG as older sources did.

new_statements.quote: In Fordata, stress is penultimate. In Yamdena stress is normally penultimate, but can shift to the ultimate syllable with the addition of plural -ar. In Kei stress is ultimate. [...] Stress and/or tone is probably contrastive in some of the Bomberai languages, though the most common pattern in our data is penultimate stress/high tone.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing statement (Milano 2025: stress lexically determined, any syllable, penultimate most common). Grimes & Edwards say the same thing at the level of the Bomberai group (contrastive stress/tone likely; penultimate most common), hedged and without naming Arguni, so it corroborates rather than adds. Not a contradiction: Milano says 'stress', G&E say 'stress and/or tone' for the group, not specifically for Arguni.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A group-level remark only: for the Austronesian languages of the Bomberai Peninsula (Onin, Sekar, Uruangnirin, Arguni, Bedoanas, Erokwanas, Irarutu, Kuri) stress and/or tone is 'probably contrastive in some' of them, and the most common pattern in the authors' data is penultimate stress / high tone. No rule is stated for Arguni itself; the book is a historical-comparative classification, not a description.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Arguni. The Arguni forms in the comparative tables (from Narfafan 2011 and Smits & Voorhoeve 1992a,b) carry acute accents, mostly on the penult (rárin, dówan, úmun, náne, rágit, púrin, gádin, twári) but also on the final syllable (ga-rúr, syá, neswá, iyáf) and two marks in tigyánáne; the book does not state what the acute marks in the Arguni data mean (its Aru-chapter convention 'unexpected stress is marked by an acute accent', printed pp. 88 and 273, is explicitly about Nivens's Aru data, and p. 88 warns that many sources give no information about their diacritics).
new_statements.identity_note: Grimes & Edwards's Arguni (ISO agf, Glottolog argu1237, -2.65 132.56; appendix A, printed p. 743 = PDF 795) is built from Narfafan 2011 (LexiRumah 'Arguni word list') and Smits & Voorhoeve 1992a,b (Anceaux wordlists); they place it in East Bomberai within Tanimbar-Bomberai (STB). Their stress remark is about 'the Bomberai languages' as a group, not any particular Arguni variety. Milano 2025 is the only Arguni-specific stress source.
